0.title: From Eden to the New Jerusalem
0.essay:
The Bible is sixty-six books, written over many centuries by many authors in many styles. Yet it tells one story. It begins in a garden and ends in a garden city. It opens with God creating the heavens and the earth, and closes with God making all things new. And at its centre stands one person: Jesus Christ.

Why the big story matters

Many Christians know individual Bible stories well — Noah’s ark, David and Goliath, Jonah and the great fish — but cannot see how they fit together. The Old Testament becomes a collection of moral examples (“be brave like David”), or a long book we quietly skip. Jesus read it very differently. “You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me” (John 5:39). After his resurrection, walking with two discouraged disciples, “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27).

Knowing the storyline changes how we read every page. A passage in Leviticus or a psalm of lament takes its place in a larger drama. We see promises made, delayed, threatened and finally kept. And we understand why the coming of Christ is not a new idea God had halfway through, but the climax everything was moving toward.

One way to hold it together

A simple thread runs through the whole Bible: God’s people, in God’s place, under God’s rule, enjoying God’s blessing. Eden had all four. The fall lost them. The rest of Scripture is the story of God restoring them — partly in Israel, decisively in Christ, and finally and fully in the new creation. Keep that thread in mind and the story becomes clear.

The six chapters

Creation and Fall — God’s good world, humanity’s rebellion, and the first promise of rescue. The Promise to Abraham — God’s answer to a cursed world begins with one man and a promise to bless all nations. A People, a Law and a Land — the exodus, Sinai, the tabernacle and the land. Kings, Prophets and Exile — the rise and fall of Israel’s kingdom, and the prophets’ hope of a new covenant. The Promise Kept in Christ — how everything finds its “yes” in Jesus. To the Nations and the New Creation — the gospel going to the ends of the earth, and the ending God has promised.

Read them in order, with a Bible open. The aim is not just to learn the outline, but to see the faithfulness of the God who wrote it — and to find your own place in his story.

1.title: Creation and Fall
1.essay:
Every story has a beginning that sets up everything else. The Bible’s first eleven chapters do exactly that: a good world, a terrible rebellion, and a promise that will take the rest of Scripture to fulfil.

The world as it was meant to be

The story begins at its high point. God speaks, and light, sky, land, sea, plants and creatures come into being. Then he makes humanity: “So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). He blesses them, gives them every plant for food and the task of filling and ruling the earth on his behalf. “And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31).

In Eden, all four parts of our thread are in place. God’s people live in God’s place, the garden he planted. They live under God’s rule, his word telling them what is good. And they enjoy his blessing and presence: the LORD God walks in the garden. This is the world God made — and the world he will one day restore, and more.

What went wrong

Then came the fall. The serpent questioned God’s word — “Did God actually say…?” — and Adam and Eve took the one fruit God had forbidden. They wanted to decide good and evil for themselves. Everything unravelled. They hid from God, blamed each other, and were driven out of the garden, away from his presence. Death entered the world.

The damage spread quickly. Their son Cain murdered his brother Abel. By Noah’s day “the earth was filled with violence” (Genesis 6:11), and God judged it with the flood. After the flood, humanity united to build a tower to “make a name for ourselves” (Genesis 11:4). God came down, confused their languages and scattered them across the earth. Pride had brought division. At the end of Genesis 11, the question hangs in the air: how will God bless a cursed world?

Grace in the middle of judgment

Yet from the very beginning, judgment is never God’s last word. In the curse on the serpent there is a promise: “I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel” (Genesis 3:15). One day a child of the woman would crush the serpent — though not without being wounded himself. Theologians call it the first gospel. From here on, the Bible is watching for that offspring.

Notice how every judgment in these chapters is followed by mercy. God clothes Adam and Eve before sending them out. He puts a protective mark on Cain. He rescues Noah and his family, and then makes a covenant with every living creature never again to destroy the earth with a flood, setting his bow in the clouds as a sign (Genesis 9:12–17). That covenant of preservation holds the world steady so that his plan of salvation can unfold. Even the scattering at Babel will one day be reversed: at Pentecost, people from many nations will hear the gospel in their own languages (Acts 2).

Why it matters for us

Genesis 1–11 explains the world we live in. It tells us why life is beautiful — we are made in God’s image, in a good creation — and why it is so broken: we have turned from God, and death, conflict and division have followed. It tells us that the problem is not our circumstances but our hearts. And it tells us that God has not given up on his world. The rest of the Bible is the story of how he brings a people back into his presence, under his rule, in a renewed creation. Everything lost in Eden will be restored.

For reflection

List as many things as you can that were lost in the fall. How does Genesis 3:15 set up the rest of the Bible? Where do you see judgment followed by grace in Genesis 1–11? How does Babel connect with Pentecost?

2.title: The Promise to Abraham
2.essay:
After the darkness of Genesis 3–11, the story suddenly narrows to one man. God’s answer to a scattered, cursed world begins with an elderly, childless couple — and a promise big enough to reach every nation on earth.

The call and the promise

“Now the LORD said to Abram, ‘Go from your country and your kindred and your father’s house to the land that I will show you. And I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and him who dishonors you I will curse, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed’” (Genesis 12:1–3).

After chapters full of curses, the word “bless” appears five times in three verses. God promises Abraham three things: a people (a great nation), a land (Canaan) and blessing — not only for Abraham, but through him for all the families of the earth. The contrast with Babel is deliberate. At Babel people tried to make a name for themselves and were scattered; now God will make Abraham’s name great and bring blessing to the scattered nations. The answer to human pride is God’s grace.

Faith counted as righteousness

Abraham was old, and Sarah was barren. Years passed with no child. When Abraham questioned God, the LORD took him outside: “Look toward heaven, and number the stars, if you are able to number them… So shall your offspring be.” And “he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:5–6). Paul builds his whole teaching of justification by faith on that verse (Romans 4:3). Abraham was not made right with God by his obedience, but by trusting God’s promise. Faith in God’s word has always been the way of salvation.

Then God bound himself by covenant in a strange ceremony. Animals were cut in two, and normally both parties would walk between the pieces, saying in effect, “May this happen to me if I break my word.” But only God, appearing as a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch, passed between them (Genesis 15:17). He took the whole obligation on himself.

The LORD will provide

After twenty-five years, Isaac was born — the child of promise. Then came the hardest test imaginable: God told Abraham to offer Isaac as a sacrifice. Abraham obeyed, trusting that God could even raise the dead (Hebrews 11:19). As he raised the knife, the angel of the LORD stopped him, and a ram caught in a thicket took Isaac’s place. Abraham called the place “The LORD will provide” (Genesis 22:14). Two thousand years later, on a hill in the same region, God did not spare his own Son. Isaac carrying the wood up the mountain, and the ram provided in his place, point straight to the cross.

The promises passed from Abraham to Isaac, then to Jacob — a schemer and deceiver whom God chose anyway, and renamed Israel — and to his twelve sons. God’s promises never depended on the worthiness of the people who received them. Genesis ends with Jacob’s family in Egypt: a small clan, waiting for God to keep his word.

The promise reaches us

Paul says that when God spoke to Abraham, Scripture “preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, ‘In you shall all the nations be blessed’” (Galatians 3:8). The promised “offspring”, he points out, is ultimately one person — Christ (Galatians 3:16). And “if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise” (Galatians 3:29). Every Gentile believer, in any country and century, is part of the answer to a promise made to an old man in the ancient Near East. Your faith in Christ is the fulfilment of Genesis 12.

For reflection

What three things did God promise Abraham? Why does Paul call Genesis 12:3 the gospel preached beforehand? How does Genesis 22 point to Christ? What does it mean for you to be a child of Abraham by faith?

3.title: A People, a Law and a Land
3.essay:
Four hundred years after Abraham, his descendants were a great nation — but slaves in Egypt. The book of Exodus tells how God rescued them, made them his people, came to live among them and brought them into the land he had promised. It became the Bible’s great picture of salvation.

Rescued by blood and power

A new Pharaoh enslaved Israel and tried to destroy their sons. But “God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham” (Exodus 2:24). He raised up Moses and sent plagues on Egypt. On the final night, each Israelite family killed a lamb and put its blood on their doorposts. “When I see the blood, I will pass over you” (Exodus 12:13). The firstborn of Egypt died; Israel’s were spared. God led his people out through the Red Sea and destroyed Pharaoh’s army behind them.

The Passover and the exodus became the pattern for everything that followed. The prophets promised a new exodus. Jesus died at Passover, and Paul calls him “our Passover lamb” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Every Christian has been through a greater exodus: rescued from slavery to sin, sheltered from judgment by the blood of the Lamb.

Grace first, then law

At Mount Sinai God made a covenant with Israel. Notice the order. He began with what he had done: “You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself” (Exodus 19:4). Only then did he call them to obey and to be “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6) — titles Peter later gives to the church (1 Peter 2:9).

The law, including the Ten Commandments, was given to a people already rescued. It was not a ladder to climb to earn God’s favour, but the shape of life for those he had redeemed. It also did something else: it revealed sin, and showed that Israel needed a better sacrifice and a better heart (Hebrews 10:1–4).

God in their midst

God commanded Israel to build the tabernacle, a portable tent where he would live among them. When it was finished, “the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” (Exodus 40:34). Something of Eden’s closeness was being restored. But only partly: God’s presence rested behind a curtain in the Most Holy Place, and sinners could approach him only through priests and sacrifices.

That dwelling of God with his people is a thread worth following through the whole Bible: from the garden, to the tabernacle, to the temple, to Christ who “dwelt among us” (John 1:14), to the church as God’s temple, and finally to the new creation, where “the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3).

Into the land

Israel’s journey was marked by grumbling and rebellion. When the people refused to trust God and enter the land, that generation died in the wilderness over forty years (Numbers 14). But God did not abandon his promise. Under Joshua, the next generation crossed the Jordan and took possession of Canaan. The book of Joshua sums it up: “Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass” (Joshua 21:45).

For a moment, the thread is pulled tight again: God’s people, in God’s place, under God’s rule, enjoying his blessing. The promise to Abraham had been kept in history. The question now is whether they will stay faithful.

Seeing ourselves in the story

When you read Exodus, you are reading your own story in picture form: slavery, a lamb, blood, rescue, a law of love, God coming to live with his people, a journey through the wilderness toward a promised home. Next time you take the Lord’s Supper, remember that it was first a Passover meal. Christ our Passover has been sacrificed, and we are on our way home.

For reflection

In what ways is your salvation like the exodus? Why was the law given after the rescue, not before? Trace God’s dwelling with his people from Eden to the new creation. How does Joshua 21:45 encourage you to trust God’s promises today?

4.title: Kings, Prophets and Exile
4.essay:
Israel had the land, the law and God’s presence. What it did not have was a heart that stayed faithful. This chapter of the story is a long, painful decline — and, in the darkest moment, the brightest promises of the Old Testament.

A people without a king

After Joshua, Israel fell into a repeating cycle: the people turned to idols, enemies oppressed them, they cried out, God raised up a judge to rescue them — and then they turned away again. The book of Judges ends with a bleak summary: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25). Israel needed a righteous king.

David and the promise of a forever king

Israel demanded a king like the nations around them. Saul began well but disobeyed God. Then God chose a shepherd boy, David, “a man after his own heart” (1 Samuel 13:14). Under David and his son Solomon, the kingdom reached its height. Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem, and God’s glory filled it.

God made a covenant with David that shaped all of Israel’s later hope. He promised that one of David’s offspring would reign for ever: “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son… And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever” (2 Samuel 7:14–16). From then on, Israel watched for a coming son of David — the Messiah, the anointed king.

Division, decline and the prophets

But Solomon turned to idols in his old age, and after his death the kingdom split in two: Israel in the north, Judah in the south. King after king led the people into idolatry and injustice. God sent prophets — Elijah, Elisha, Amos, Hosea, Isaiah, Jeremiah and many more — to call them back. They warned of judgment, pleaded for repentance, and spoke of a future restoration. Mostly they were ignored, mocked or persecuted.

Judgment came. The northern kingdom fell to Assyria in 722 BC. In 586 BC Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and the temple, and carried the people of Judah into exile. It looked as though every promise had failed. God’s people were out of God’s place. The temple, where God had dwelt, lay in ruins. The line of David seemed cut off.

Hope in the dark

Yet it was precisely then that the prophets spoke their greatest promises. Isaiah announced a child who would bear God’s own names: “For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6). He would sit on David’s throne and reign for ever in justice.

Jeremiah promised a new covenant, unlike the one Israel had broken: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts… For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more” (Jeremiah 31:33–34). Ezekiel saw a valley of dry bones — Israel in exile, utterly hopeless — and watched as God’s breath brought them to life, with the promise, “I will put my Spirit within you, and you shall live” (Ezekiel 37:14). Isaiah spoke of a servant who would suffer and bear the sins of many.

Some exiles returned to rebuild Jerusalem and the temple. But the glory did not return as before, no son of David took the throne, and the Old Testament ends still waiting.

What this chapter teaches

Israel’s history proves that the deepest problem is the human heart. The law, the temple, prophets and kings could not change it. Israel’s three great offices — prophet, priest and king — all failed in different ways, pointing to someone who would fulfil all three perfectly. And the new covenant promised what nothing else could: a new heart, forgiveness and the Spirit.

The books of Kings can feel depressing — king after king doing evil. But read them alongside Isaiah 9 and they become something else: the long preparation for the perfect King. Like Daniel, who read Jeremiah in exile and prayed for God to act (Daniel 9), we learn to live faithfully while we wait for God to keep his word.

For reflection

Why did Israel’s kings fail, and what did their failure point to? How is the promise to David fulfilled in Jesus? What is new about the new covenant in Jeremiah 31? How does Ezekiel 37 give hope to someone who feels spiritually dead?

5.title: The Promise Kept in Christ
5.essay:
After centuries of waiting, a voice rang out in Galilee: “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel” (Mark 1:15). Everything the Old Testament had promised was arriving in one person.

Every promise finds its “yes”

“For all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20). Trace the threads of the story so far and they all lead to Jesus. He is the offspring of the woman who crushes the serpent. He is the offspring of Abraham in whom all the nations are blessed. He is the prophet like Moses, the Passover lamb and the true temple where God dwells with us. He is the Son of David, the King whose kingdom will never end. He is the suffering servant of Isaiah who bears our sins, and the one who pours out the promised Spirit. He brings the new covenant, written on hearts, with sins remembered no more.

The true Israel

Jesus does not only fulfil promises; he relives Israel’s story and succeeds where Israel failed. Like Israel, he came out of Egypt (Matthew 2:15). Like Israel, he passed through the waters, at his baptism, and was tested in the wilderness — but where Israel grumbled and fell, he stood firm, answering every temptation with the Scriptures Israel had been given (Matthew 4:1–11). Israel was God’s vine that bore bad fruit; Jesus is “the true vine” (John 15:1). He is the faithful Son that Israel, and Adam before them, never were.

The cross and the empty tomb

At the cross, the serpent struck the heel of the woman’s offspring: Jesus died. But by his death he crushed the serpent’s head, defeated the devil and paid in full for the sins of his people. On the third day he rose. It is no accident that the new creation began in a garden, with a man mistaken for the gardener. The story that went wrong in a garden starts to be put right in one.

Reading the Old Testament with Christ at the centre

On the evening of the resurrection, two disciples walked to Emmaus, confused and disappointed. The risen Jesus joined them unrecognised and said, “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” Then, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he showed them himself in all the Scriptures (Luke 24:25–27). Later he told the gathered disciples that everything written about him in the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms had to be fulfilled, and that repentance and forgiveness would be proclaimed in his name to all nations (Luke 24:44–47).

This does not mean hunting for hidden meanings in every detail of the Old Testament. It means following the storyline, the promises and the patterns God himself built into history — as the apostles did. When the Ethiopian official asked Philip who Isaiah 53 was about, “beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus” (Acts 8:35).

Already, and not yet

In Christ the kingdom has truly come. But it has not yet come in its fullness. We live between his first coming and his second: the King reigns, the decisive victory is won, the Spirit is poured out — and yet sin, suffering and death remain until he returns. Much has changed with Christ: the sacrifices and food laws are fulfilled, the people of God now include all nations, and every believer has the Spirit. But it is one story, and one God who keeps every word.

That changes how we read our Bibles. A man who grew up hearing David and Goliath as a lesson in courage — “be brave like David” — hears a sermon showing that David is a picture of Christ, the true champion who fights the battle his people cannot win. The Bible stops being mainly about us being heroes. It becomes the story of the hero who rescues us.

For reflection

Name five Old Testament promises or patterns fulfilled in Christ. How did Jesus relive and succeed in Israel’s story? What does it mean for you that all God’s promises are “yes” in Christ? How can you read the Old Testament with Christ at the centre without forcing meanings onto it?

6.title: To the Nations and the New Creation
6.essay:
The story is not over. We are living in its final chapter: the gospel going out to the nations, the church gathering from every people, and the whole of creation waiting for the ending God has promised.

Babel reversed

After his resurrection, Jesus told his disciples, “you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (Acts 1:8). Then he ascended, and angels promised that he would come again in the same way. Ten days later, at Pentecost, the Spirit was poured out, and Jews gathered from many nations heard the apostles declaring God’s works in their own languages (Acts 2:5–11). The scattering of Babel had begun to be reversed.

The book of Acts follows the map Jesus gave: from Jerusalem, to Samaria, to Gentiles, and on to Rome, the capital of the world. The promise to Abraham — that all the families of the earth would be blessed — was being fulfilled before the apostles’ eyes. In Antioch, believers from Jewish and Gentile backgrounds worshipped together and sent out Paul and Barnabas to take the gospel further still (Acts 13:1–3).

One new people

Paul calls this a mystery hidden for ages and now revealed: “This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel” (Ephesians 3:6). The church does not replace Israel as though God changed his plans. Believing Gentiles are grafted into the one olive tree of God’s people (Romans 11:17–24). And through this mixed and unlikely community, God’s manifold wisdom is displayed even to the powers in the heavenly places (Ephesians 3:10).

A church in a multicultural city may have members from twenty nations. Around the Lord’s Table, a visitor looks at the faces and is moved: this is a small picture of the end of the story.

How the story ends

The Bible’s last book lifts the curtain on the ending. John sees “a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb” (Revelation 7:9). Abraham’s promise is fulfilled to the last nation.

Then he sees a new heaven and a new earth, and the holy city coming down from God. “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more” (Revelation 21:3–4). The river of life flows, the tree of life stands, the curse is gone, and God’s servants “will see his face” (Revelation 22:4).

Our thread is pulled tight for ever: God’s people, in God’s place, under God’s rule, enjoying his blessing. The story that began in a garden ends in a garden city, far more glorious than Eden. Christ reigns now from heaven, and when he returns there will be the resurrection of the dead, the final judgment and the new creation. Faithful Christians differ on some details of the order of those last events (the End Times Models study explains the views), but not on the ending itself.

Your place in the story

Every Christian has a part in this story. We are not spectators but participants, living between the resurrection and the return of Christ. Our calling is to bear witness — in our homes, workplaces and neighbourhoods, and through supporting the gospel’s spread to the ends of the earth — and to live now as citizens of the world to come. We suffer, we pray, we hope, and we wait. And we know how the story ends.

For reflection

How does Pentecost reverse Babel? Why is a church of Jews and Gentiles so important in Ephesians 3? How does Revelation 7:9 fulfil the promise to Abraham? What is your part in the big story of the Bible right now?
